discoveries: (1) Inside a sandbox `/dev/shm` is a separate, empty tmpfs (device 95 here, 65 for the lead), so a lock there is not shared. (2) The lock on an existing file in `/tmp` is shared: it opens read-only, and a `flock` on that read-only descriptor conflicts with the outside holder (EAGAIN). (3) A sandboxed session cannot create a new file in `/tmp` (EROFS), so the machine lock file must already exist. (4) The sandbox is a separate pid namespace and `/proc/locks` there was empty (0 lines), so an outside holder cannot be shown; a sandboxed rebuild can only say "holder not known". (5) Today's rebuild runs `gitleaks stdin …` once per indexed file, inside the lexical stage.
risks: (a) If a future implementation ignores an unreadable `rebuild.yaml` (the not-YAML, not-a-map and empty-lock cases) and falls back to the default, that case would take the machine's real lock, or wait on it for up to its 60 s limit. The test cannot prevent this. (b) The live-record checks accept a small set of key names for each part, because the design names those parts only in words. (c) The slow case needs the planted gitleaks command line, cut to 200 characters, to still contain "gitleaks". It does at today's temp path lengths (about 150 characters to that word).
lessons: Plant a slow stage with a `gitleaks` stand-in first on PATH that sleeps on its first call (the paths are written into the script, so environment cleaning does not affect it). A process that holds the lock must be a sibling of the rebuild, not pytest itself: pytest is the rebuild's ancestor, so its hold would count as "held by the caller". Leaving the code-graph tool off PATH makes the code-index stage behave the same inside and outside a sandbox.
